quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Prompt Basics and Framework
quizzes.intro: Check whether you understand what prompts are and how the five-part framework works.

questions.prompt: What is a prompt in generative AI?

options.text: A secret password that unlocks a hidden model mode
The instruction or input that steers the model toward a useful output
A guarantee that the model cannot make mistakes
Only a single-word keyword with no context

questions.explanation: A prompt is the input that communicates task, context, and standards to the model.

wrongExplanations.a: Prompting is communication design, not secret passwords.
wrongExplanations.c: No prompt removes all possibility of error.
wrongExplanations.d: Useful prompts often include context, constraints, and format.

questions.prompt: Which set best represents the five-part beginner framework?

options.text: Goal, context, constraints, examples, output format
Font, color, emoji, slogan, hashtag
Password, token, seed, temperature only
Guess, regenerate, ignore, publish

questions.explanation: Those five parts help diagnose and strengthen most beginner prompts.

wrongExplanations.b: Visual decoration is not the core prompting framework.
wrongExplanations.c: Those are system parameters, not the communication framework.
wrongExplanations.d: That is an anti-pattern, not a framework.

questions.prompt: Why does audience specification improve outputs?

options.text: Because models refuse to write without an audience label
Because audience changes vocabulary, examples, depth, and tone
Because audience replaces the need for a goal
Because audience guarantees factual accuracy

questions.explanation: Audience steers communication choices that make content usable for real readers.

wrongExplanations.a: Models can write without it, but often produce generic results.
wrongExplanations.c: You still need a clear goal.
wrongExplanations.d: Audience fit and factual accuracy are different issues.

options.text: Write about AI.
Write a 700-word beginner article explaining AI with an analogy, three examples, limitations, calm tone, and H2 markdown headings.
Make it viral.
You are an expert. Do something impressive.

questions.explanation: The strong prompt specifies deliverable, audience level, structure, tone, and format.

wrongExplanations.c: Vague success criteria invite generic hype.
wrongExplanations.d: Role theater without a concrete task is weak.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of constraints in a prompt?

options.text: To make the model fail intentionally
To steer boundaries such as length, tone, forbidden content, and required elements
To replace examples and goals
To force the model to invent statistics

questions.explanation: Constraints are steering wheels that keep outputs usable and safer.

wrongExplanations.a: Constraints improve fit; they are not sabotage.
wrongExplanations.d: Good constraints often forbid invented statistics.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Examples, Iteration, and Risk
quizzes.intro: Apply example design, revision discipline, evaluation, and hallucination awareness.

questions.prompt: When are few-shot examples most useful?

options.text: When you want to avoid specifying any format forever
When you need to teach a specific style, structure, or transformation
When factual grounding is unnecessary in medicine
When you have no goal at all

questions.explanation: Examples show the model what good output looks like more concretely than abstract adjectives.

wrongExplanations.a: Examples help format; they do not remove the need for clarity forever.
wrongExplanations.c: High-stakes domains need grounding and review, not fewer safeguards.
wrongExplanations.d: Examples cannot substitute for a missing goal.

questions.prompt: Which revision request is most effective?

options.text: Try again.
Keep the structure, cut 20%, replace vague claims with concrete examples, and remove hype adjectives in paragraph two.
Make it better somehow.
Ignore all previous constraints.

questions.explanation: Specific critique preserves strengths and repairs exact weaknesses.

wrongExplanations.a: Too vague to guide a controlled revision.

questions.prompt: What is a practical way to reduce hallucinations in factual tasks?

options.text: Ask for more confidence and no sources
Ground the prompt in approved notes and require unknowns to be stated rather than guessed
Remove all constraints
Request invented citations for credibility

questions.explanation: Grounding plus anti-guessing instructions reduce fluent fabrication risk.

wrongExplanations.d: Invented citations are a classic failure mode.

questions.prompt: Why use an evaluation rubric on AI outputs?

options.text: Because fluent text is always correct
Because rubrics check goal fit, constraints, faithfulness, and usefulness beyond surface polish
Because rubrics replace human accountability
Because rubrics make examples unnecessary in every case

questions.explanation: Rubrics protect you from mistaking fluency for quality.

wrongExplanations.a: Fluency can hide weak or false content.
wrongExplanations.c: Humans remain accountable for high-stakes use.
wrongExplanations.d: Examples and rubrics solve different problems.

questions.prompt: What should a model do when the answer is not in provided notes?

options.text: Guess confidently to be helpful
State that it is not found or unknown, according to your constraint
Invent a plausible citation
Change the user goal silently

questions.explanation: Explicit unknown behavior is safer than helpful-sounding fabrication.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Workflows, Templates, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Use the full lesson. Focus on workflows, templates, and responsible judgment.

questions.prompt: Why break complex work into multi-step prompt workflows?

options.text: Because models cannot follow any single instruction
Because smaller stages are easier to specify, evaluate, and revise than one mega-prompt
Because workflows forbid examples
Because multi-step prompts eliminate all risk automatically

questions.explanation: Decomposition improves control and quality management across complex deliverables.

wrongExplanations.a: Models can follow single instructions; complex tasks still benefit from staging.
wrongExplanations.d: Risk still requires grounding and review.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a reusable prompt template?

options.text: Only emojis and slogans
Fields for goal, audience, context, constraints, sources, format, and evaluation criteria
A demand to invent missing data
A rule never to state uncertainty

questions.explanation: Reusable templates encode the framework so quality starts higher every time.

wrongExplanations.a: Decoration is not a template foundation.
wrongExplanations.c: Templates should reduce invention risk, not encourage it.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows mature prompt judgment?

options.text: If it sounds fluent, ship it to customers immediately
Match prompting method to task risk, evaluate outputs, and keep humans accountable for high-stakes use
One mega-prompt should always do research, writing, and legal review
Confidential data can be pasted anywhere if the prompt is polite

questions.explanation: Mature practice balances usefulness with evaluation, grounding, and responsibility.

wrongExplanations.a: Fluency is not a ship criteria.
wrongExplanations.c: Complex and high-stakes work needs staged control and human review.
wrongExplanations.d: Privacy and tool approval rules still apply.

questions.prompt: For a coding assistant prompt, what should you include?

options.text: Only 'write code' with no language or examples
Language, constraints, input/output examples, and edge cases
A request to invent APIs that might exist
No mention of failure behavior

questions.explanation: Precise technical briefs dramatically improve code usefulness and reduce fabrication.

wrongExplanations.a: Underspecified coding asks produce fragile results.
wrongExplanations.c: Invented APIs are a common failure mode.
wrongExplanations.d: Failure and edge-case behavior should be specified.

questions.prompt: What is the best response when stakeholder requests are vague?

options.text: Prompt the model immediately with the vague ask unchanged
Translate the ask into a clear brief by clarifying audience, decision, scope, and definition of done
Ask the model to invent stakeholder goals silently
Skip evaluation because stakeholders are in a hurry

questions.explanation: Briefing clarity before prompting prevents fluent answers to the wrong problem.

wrongExplanations.c: Silent invention of goals creates misalignment.
wrongExplanations.d: Speed without clarity creates rework and risk.

questions.prompt: Which habit best turns prompting into durable skill?

options.text: Collecting secret phrases without reviewing outputs
Building templates and workflows, evaluating with rubrics, and recording failure modes
Never saving successful prompts
Assuming model updates remove the need for constraints

questions.explanation: Libraries, workflows, evaluation, and failure logs create compounding craft.

wrongExplanations.a: Secret phrases without evaluation are brittle.
wrongExplanations.c: Successful prompts should be reused and refined.
wrongExplanations.d: Better models still benefit from clear constraints and review.
